cmimc-2016-geometry-01.title: Drop to the midpoint
cmimc-2016-geometry-01.body:
The side length is $50+30=80$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$; then $AM=40\sqrt3$ and $MP=40-30=10$. By Pythagoras, $AP^2=(40\sqrt3)^2+10^2=4800+100=4900$, so $AP=70$.

**Answer: 70**

cmimc-2016-geometry-02.title: Midline
cmimc-2016-geometry-02.body:
Let $M,N$ be the midpoints of the legs $AD$, $BC$; they are the centers of the two circles, each of radius $\frac{15}2$. The circles are tangent (externally, since they lie on opposite sides), so $MN=\frac{15}2+\frac{15}2=15$. But $MN$ is the midline of the trapezoid, equal to the average of the bases. Therefore the area is (height)$\cdot MN=7\cdot15=105$.

**Answer: 105**

cmimc-2016-geometry-03.title: Angle bisector theorem with areas
cmimc-2016-geometry-03.body:
$[BCP]=72-27=45$, so $\frac{AB}{BC}=\frac{AP}{PC}=\frac{[ABP]}{[BCP]}=\frac{27}{45}=\frac35$. Similarly $[BCQ]=72-32=40$ and $\frac{AC}{BC}=\frac{AQ}{QB}=\frac{32}{40}=\frac45$.

So the sides are in ratio $AB:AC:BC=3:4:5$: a right triangle with right angle at $A$. With $AB=3x$, $AC=4x$: area $6x^2=72$, $x^2=12$. Then $BC=5x=5\sqrt{12}=10\sqrt3$ and $m+n=13$.

**Answer: 13**

cmimc-2016-geometry-04.title: Unfold the icosahedron
cmimc-2016-geometry-04.body:
Unfold the faces along the path into a strip of equilateral triangles (the net of the icosahedron). The shortest path from a vertex to the opposite vertex is the straight segment between them in the net. It is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are the height of one face, $2\sqrt3$ (for edge $4$), and $\frac52$ of an edge, $10$.

So the distance is $\sqrt{10^2+(2\sqrt3)^2}=\sqrt{112}$ and $n=112$. (An exhaustive search over all unfoldings of face sequences confirms $\sqrt{112}$ is the minimum.)

**Answer: 112**

cmimc-2016-geometry-05.title: Parallelogram law in 3D
cmimc-2016-geometry-05.body:
Let the edge vectors be $\mathbf x,\mathbf y,\mathbf z$. The four space diagonals are $\mathbf x\pm\mathbf y\pm\mathbf z$ (up to sign). Applying the parallelogram law $|\mathbf u+\mathbf v|^2+|\mathbf u-\mathbf v|^2=2|\mathbf u|^2+2|\mathbf v|^2$ three times gives

$|\mathbf x+\mathbf y+\mathbf z|^2+|\mathbf x+\mathbf y-\mathbf z|^2+|\mathbf x-\mathbf y+\mathbf z|^2+|-\mathbf x+\mathbf y+\mathbf z|^2=4(|\mathbf x|^2+|\mathbf y|^2+|\mathbf z|^2).$

(Indeed, $\mathbf x+\mathbf y$ and $\mathbf z$ give $|\mathbf x+\mathbf y+\mathbf z|^2+|\mathbf x+\mathbf y-\mathbf z|^2=2|\mathbf x+\mathbf y|^2+2|\mathbf z|^2$, similarly for $\mathbf x-\mathbf y$, and then add and use the law once more on $\mathbf x\pm\mathbf y$.)

Therefore $4(x^2+y^2+z^2)=15^2+17^2+21^2+23^2=225+289+441+529=1484$, so $x^2+y^2+z^2=371$.

**Answer: 371**

cmimc-2016-geometry-06.title: Orthocenter and circumcircle
cmimc-2016-geometry-06.body:
$P$ is the orthocenter of $\triangle ABC$. Since $DA\parallel BC$ and $DC\parallel AB$, we get $DA\perp AP$ and $DC\perp CP$, so $DAPC$ is cyclic with diameter $DP$. This circle is the circumcircle of $\triangle DAC$, congruent to that of $\triangle ABC$, so $PD=2R$ where $R$ is the circumradius of $ABC$.

Also $PB=2R\cos B$ (distance from a vertex to the orthocenter), and $AC=2R\sin B$ by the Law of Sines. Hence $AC^2+PB^2=(2R)^2=PD^2$, so

$AC^2=821^2-700^2=(821-700)(821+700)=121\cdot1521=(11\cdot39)^2$, giving $AC=429$.

**Answer: 429**

cmimc-2016-geometry-07.title: Radical axis
cmimc-2016-geometry-07.body:
$X,Y$ lie on the circle $\Omega$ with diameter $BC$ and on $\omega$, so line $XY$ is the radical axis of $\omega$ and $\Omega$; the condition says $I$ lies on it, so $I$ has equal power with respect to both circles.

With $a=BC$, $s$ the semiperimeter and $r$ the inradius: the power of $I$ w.r.t. $\omega$ is $-r^2$ (inside), and w.r.t. $\Omega$ it is $IM^2-\frac{a^2}4$ where $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. Writing $D$ for the touch point on $BC$ ($BD=s-b$), $IM^2=r^2+\left(\frac a2-(s-b)\right)^2$. Equating gives

$2r^2=(s-b)(s-c)$.

Since $r^2=\frac{(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}{s}$, this becomes $2(s-a)=s$, i.e. $s=2(s-a)$, so $b+c=3a$. Thus $BC=\frac{80+97}3=59$.

**Answer: 59**

cmimc-2016-geometry-08.title: Construct a congruent triangle
cmimc-2016-geometry-08.body:
Here $\angle ABC=100^\circ$ and $AB=BC$, so $\angle BAC=40^\circ$. Build point $X$ outside $\triangle ABC$ with $\triangle AXC\cong\triangle BCD$ (possible since $AC=BD$; $AX=BC$, $CX=CD$).

Then $\angle XAC=\angle CBD=20^\circ$, so $\angle BAX=40^\circ+20^\circ=60^\circ$, and $AX=BC=BA$, so $\triangle ABX$ is equilateral. Then $\angle CBX=100^\circ-60^\circ=40^\circ$ with $BC=BX$, so $\angle BXC=70^\circ$. Therefore $\angle BCD=\angle AXC=\angle AXB+\angle BXC=60^\circ+70^\circ=130^\circ$.

**Answer: 130**

cmimc-2016-geometry-08.title: Coordinates
cmimc-2016-geometry-08.body: Put $B=(0,0)$, $C=(1,0)$, $A=(\cos100^\circ,\sin100^\circ)$, $D=AC\cdot(\cos20^\circ,\sin20^\circ)$. Computing the angle at $C$ numerically gives $130^\circ$.

cmimc-2016-geometry-09.title: Homothety and coordinates
cmimc-2016-geometry-09.body:
Scale down by $5$: $AB=13$, $BC=14$, $CA=15$. Let $\kappa$ be the incircle (radius $4$) and $\Gamma$ the circle with diameter $BC$ (radius $7$, center $M$). The homothety taking $\omega$ to $\kappa$ is centered at $A$, and the one taking $\omega$ to $\Gamma$ is centered at $X$; by Monge's theorem $AX$ passes through the exsimilicenter $P$ of $\kappa$ and $\Gamma$.

Put $M$ at the origin and $BC$ on the $x$-axis, so $A=(-2,12)$ and $I=(-1,4)$. The external center $P$ divides so that $PI:PM=4:7$, which gives $P=\left(-\frac73,\frac{28}3\right)$. The slope of $AP$ is $8$, so line $AX$ meets $BC$ at $D$ with $DM=\frac72$ and $X$ lies on the semicircle below $BC$ at $X_0X=8t$ where $X_0D=t$. Pythagoras in $\triangle MX_0X$: $\left(t+\frac72\right)^2+(8t)^2=49$, giving $t=\frac7{10}$, and then $AX=\frac{11\sqrt{65}}5$.

Scaling back up by $5$: $AX=11\sqrt{65}$, so $m+n=76$. (Direct numerical solution of the tangency conditions gives $AX^2=7865=11^2\cdot65$.)

**Answer: 76**

cmimc-2016-geometry-10.title: Key lemmas
cmimc-2016-geometry-10.body:
Let $D$ be the touch point of $\omega$ on $BC$ and $a=BC$, $s$ the semiperimeter. One shows (angle chasing) that $X$, $D$, $I$ are collinear with $XI\perp BC$, that $AX\parallel BC$, and that $P$ is the intersection of $EF$ with $BC$. If $Q$ is the second intersection of $\Omega$ with the circle $(AEF)$, then $Q$ lies on $PN$ and $PQ\cdot PX=PE\cdot PF=PD^2$, while $PQ\cdot PN=PB\cdot PC$.

Hence $\frac{PN}{PX}=\frac{PB\cdot PC}{PD^2}$. Since $(P,D;B,C)$ is harmonic, $\frac{PB}{PC}=\frac{DB}{DC}=\frac{s-b}{s-c}$, giving $PB=\frac{a(s-b)}{b-c}$, $PC=\frac{a(s-c)}{b-c}$, and $PD=\frac{2(s-b)(s-c)}{b-c}$. Therefore

$\frac{PN}{PX}=\frac{a^2}{4(s-b)(s-c)}=\frac{16^2}{4\cdot9\cdot7}=\frac{64}{63}$ with $s=24$, $b=17$, $c=15$.

So $\frac{XN}{PX}=\frac{PN}{PX}-1=\frac1{63}$ and $\frac{PX}{XN}=63$. (A coordinate computation confirms this value.)

**Answer: 63**
